title: Severe epigastric pain and vomiting — recognise the danger and explain the immediate plan

blocks.text: Severe epigastric pain and vomiting — recognise the danger and explain the immediate plan

Round 5 • PACES Station 2: acute consultation • Skills C communication, E clinical judgement, F managing concerns, G welfare (with focused A/B/D where relevant) • 20 minutes • Educational examiner-style encounter • Prepared 14 October 2026 • Not an official PACES mark scheme

A 49-year-old presents with sudden severe epigastric pain radiating to the back and persistent vomiting. Take a focused acute history, assess severity and discuss the immediate management of suspected acute pancreatitis.

sections.heading: 4. The Hook and the Examiner Trap

blocks.text: Hook: Acute pancreatitis, supported by typical pain and raised lipase. Trap: No routine prophylactic antibiotics for uncomplicated acute pancreatitis or sterile necrosis. Escalate organ failure, shock or cholangitis; do not automatically keep patients nil-by-mouth without reason.

rows: “First I need to check if this is affecting your immediate safety.”
“I have a working diagnosis but need to exclude dangerous alternatives.”
Perforated ulcer, myocardial infarction, biliary sepsis, mesenteric ischaemia and ruptured aneurysm may cause dangerous acute abdominal pain.
The blood test and pain pattern suggest an inflamed pancreas. We will control pain, correct dehydration while monitoring you, and look for gallstones or another cause.

ABCDE and early analgesia, antiemetics, judicious IV crystalloid guided by clinical reassessment, oxygen only if required, FBC, U&E, glucose, LFTs, calcium, triglycerides where appropriate and gallbladder ultrasound. Assess organ failure and repeated observations; plan nutrition and gallstone management if implicated.
Antibiotics do not help uncomplicated pancreatic inflammation. If infection or blocked infected bile ducts are suspected, that changes our plan.
Check patient priorities, understanding and follow-up.
Dismisses severe epigastric pain and vomiting
Suspects acute pancreatitis and checks instability and peritonitis
Keeps alternative emergencies including perforation, ischaemia and MI in view
Assumes alcohol as cause based on history alone
Asks about gallstones, alcohol, medicines, hypercalcaemia and lipids
Investigates biliary cause and avoids premature diagnostic closure
Orders CT routinely as first-line confirmation
Checks serum lipase or amylase and supportive labs
Uses imaging selectively when clinical and enzyme findings do not confirm diagnosis
Prescribes either no fluids or unrestricted fluid boluses
Gives analgesia, antiemetics and IV fluids tailored to physiology with reassessment
Tracks urine output, organ function and fluid-overload risk
Gives prophylactic antibiotics for uncomplicated pancreatitis
Distinguishes confirmed infection or cholangitis requiring targeted treatment
Keeps all patients nil by mouth until enzymes normal
Allows oral intake when clinically tolerated and supports enteral nutrition in more severe cases
Recognises early enteral support within 72 hours in severe/moderately severe disease

blocks.text: Opening line: “The pain goes right through to my back. I have vomited all morning. Will I need surgery?” The actor is concerned but able to engage unless the examiner introduces deterioration. Release only history in the candidate brief; do not volunteer a diagnostic label. Ask “Why do you need to do that?” after proposed treatment. Acknowledge clear, compassionate explanations.

R2/R3: Missing the characteristic pattern or treating a suggested cause as proven. Perforated ulcer, myocardial infarction, biliary sepsis, mesenteric ischaemia and ruptured aneurysm may cause dangerous acute abdominal pain.

R4/R5: Omitting the named critical action. No routine prophylactic antibiotics for uncomplicated acute pancreatitis or sterile necrosis. Escalate organ failure, shock or cholangitis; do not automatically keep patients nil-by-mouth without reason.
R6: Saying “we will monitor” without a comprehensible explanation of what is being done.
“I will check whether this patient is physiologically unstable before proceeding.”

“The key safety issue is: No routine prophylactic antibiotics for uncomplicated acute pancreatitis or sterile necrosis. Escalate organ failure, shock or cholangitis; do not automatically keep patients nil-by-mouth without reason.”
“Let me explain why the next investigation and treatment cannot wait.”

Confirm suspected acute pancreatitis by compatible symptoms and raised lipase/amylase, using CT selectively when enzymes are non-diagnostic. NICE NG104 advises against prophylactic antibiotics and against routine nil-by-mouth; provide nutrition where tolerated and early enteral feeding in severe disease. Reassess fluid prescriptions frequently and do not assume alcohol causation solely because the patient drinks.

THINK: Acute pancreatitis, supported by typical pain and raised lipase. SAY: The blood test and pain pattern suggest an inflamed pancreas. We will control pain, correct dehydration while monitoring you, and look for gallstones or another cause. DO: ABCDE and early analgesia, antiemetics, judicious IV crystalloid guided by clinical reassessment, oxygen only if required, FBC, U&E, glucose, LFTs, calcium, triglycerides where appropriate and gallbladder ultrasound. Assess organ failure and repeated observations; plan nutrition and gallstone management if implicated. NUMBERS: 20-minute encounter. TRAP: No routine prophylactic antibiotics for uncomplicated acute pancreatitis or sterile necrosis. Escalate organ failure, shock or cholangitis; do not automatically keep patients nil-by-mouth without reason. FINISH: Antibiotics do not help uncomplicated pancreatic inflammation. If infection or blocked infected bile ducts are suspected, that changes our plan.
NICE NG104 pancreatitis, published 2018 — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng104/chapter/Recommendations — supports treatment/urgency decisions; accessed 14 October 2026.
